name: Hinduism
idea: Hindu texts hold many of these ideas in their own terms: karma as action and its results, karma yoga as acting for duty without clinging to reward, dana as giving, seva as service, and the old teaching that a guest, even a stranger, is to be honored. The Bhagavad Gita praises a gift made to someone who cannot repay it. Schools differ on who or what weighs deeds (Ishvara, the law of karma itself, or the self), and Hinduism does not usually describe life as a single test; many streams see it as a long course of learning across births.

passages.text: Find full reward Of doing right in right! Let right deeds be Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
passages.translation: Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885 (public domain)

passages.text: Being of equal grace to comrades, friends, Chance-comers, strangers, lovers, enemies, Aliens and kinsmen; loving all alike, Evil or good.
passages.translation: Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885 (public domain)

passages.text: Who hateth nought Of all which lives, living himself benign, Compassionate, from arrogance exempt, Exempt from love of self, unchangeable By good or ill; patient, contented, firm
passages.translation: Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885 (public domain)

passages.text: The gift lovingly given, when one shall say "Now must I gladly give!" when he who takes Can render nothing back; made in due place, Due time, and to a meet recipient, Is gift of Sattwan, fair and profitable.
passages.translation: Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial, 1885 (public domain)

practices.do: Give quietly to someone who cannot repay
practices.how: Practice dana by handing food or money to a person in need and telling no one. The Gita counts a gift that expects nothing back as the purest kind.

practices.do: Offer one task, then release the result
practices.how: Before one piece of work, dedicate it to God or to duty, then let go of praise or outcome. This is karma yoga as the Gita describes it.

practices.do: Treat a stranger as an honored guest
practices.how: Offer water, a meal, or a seat to a visitor or someone passing by, in the spirit of atithi devo bhava, the guest as divine.
Serve at a temple meal, a food bank, or a community kitchen this week, without seeking a role or credit.

practices.do: Keep one day free of harsh words
practices.how: Practice ahimsa in speech: for a single day, say nothing that wounds, online or off, even when no one would notice.

ask: How does my tradition ask me to act when no one will ever know and nothing will come back to me?
In my school, who or what weighs our deeds: Ishvara, the law of karma itself, or the self within?
How do I hold the Gita's detachment from results together with real care for the people my actions affect?
caveat: Schools such as Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita, and the Mimamsa and Samkhya traditions read karma, God, and the purpose of life differently, and Hindu teachers differ on all of this. This guide does not claim Hinduism teaches that life is a test; it points to teachings a believer may recognize in their own terms.
